cases.n: West Africa 'sex for aid' — UNHCR/Save the Children report and OIOS investigation
cases.place: Refugee camps, Guéckédou area (Guinea), Liberia and Sierra Leone
cases.victims_note: UNHCR/Save the Children UK field mission interviewed about 1,500 people; OIOS fully investigated 43 cases
cases.who: Aid workers (UN agencies, national and international NGOs), peacekeepers and community leaders
cases.d: A joint UNHCR and Save the Children UK mission reported in early 2002 that refugee children in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone were being sexually exploited by employees of NGOs, UNHCR and other UN bodies, and by peacekeepers, often in exchange for food and aid. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services then fully investigated 43 cases and substantiated 10, including the rape of a 14-year-old refugee girl in a Guinean camp and a UN Volunteer's sexual relationship with a girl of about 15 in Guéckédou; one substantiated case involved a peacekeeper, who was repatriated. OIOS (October 2002) found no allegation against a UN staff member substantiated and said it found no evidence of 'widespread' abuse; Save the Children UK replied that nothing the UN found made it think it was wrong.
cases.cite: OIOS, Investigation into sexual exploitation of refugees by aid workers in West Africa, UN doc A/57/465, 11 October 2002; Wikipedia 'Sexual exploitation and abuse in humanitarian response' (summarising UNHCR/SCF-UK report, Feb 2002)

cases.n: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
cases.who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
cases.d: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.
cases.cite: Report of the Secretary-General on the activities of OIOS: investigation into SEA in MONUC, UN doc A/59/661, 5 January 2005; A/59/710 (Zeid report), 24 March 2005

cases.n: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.place: Martissant and other contingent locations, Port-au-Prince
cases.victims_note: AP (2017) counted at least 9 children in UN files; OIOS said acts against children were 'frequent'
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.cover: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 members accused in November 2007 and 108 (incl. 3 officers) sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.
cases.d: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'MINUSTAH' and 'Sexual abuse scandal in Haiti' (citing OIOS findings and AP, 12 April 2017)

cases.n: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
cases.victims_note: UN-commissioned confidential report (leaked April 2015) cited at least about ten children; boys aged 9–13 among them
cases.who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
cases.cover: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.
cases.d: A confidential report commissioned by the UN human rights office, made public by The Guardian on 29 April 2015, recorded accounts that 16 French soldiers had sexually abused at least about ten children in Bangui between December 2013 and June 2014, including boys aged 9 to 13 in exchange for food or money near the airport camp. French investigating judges issued a dismissal (non-lieu) on 11 January 2018 for insufficient charges; the Paris prosecutor said it 'cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged. CAR authorities said they deplored the decision.
cases.cite: French Wikipedia 'Opération Sangaris' (citing The Guardian 29 Apr 2015, AFP, decision of 11 Jan 2018)

cases.n: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations
cases.victims_note: 136 alleged victims initially identified in two allegations; the 2016 UN data tables list 46 child victims for Burundi and 43 for Gabon contingent allegations
cases.who: UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in CAR (MINUSCA) military contingents from Burundi and Gabon
cases.d: The Secretary-General's 2017 report states that two allegations recorded in MINUSCA, concerning incidents in Dékoa and military personnel from Gabon and Burundi, led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims and accounted for 48% of all victims recorded in 2016. Investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.
cases.cite: Report of the Secretary-General, Special measures for protection from SEA, UN doc A/71/818, 28 Feb 2017 (annex tables); Wikipedia 'Sexual abuse by UN peacekeepers'

cases.n: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
cases.victims_note: 8 cases documented by HRW, including a 14-year-old girl
cases.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
cases.d: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.
cases.cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Central African Republic: Rape by Peacekeepers', 4 February 2016

cases.n: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
cases.place: Central African Republic (deployment areas incl. Ouaka)
cases.victims_note: 807 = size of the battalion, not number of accused
cases.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
cases.d: An 807-strong FARDC battalion deployed to MINUSCA in 2015 faced allegations including child sexual exploitation and abuse; in January 2016 the UN announced it would be repatriated, citing failure to meet vetting and preparedness requirements. The 2016 UN data list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA with 15 child victims.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'MINUSCA'; UN doc A/71/818 annex tables (2016 allegations)

cases.n: MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021)
cases.victims_note: UN did not give ages in the announcement; the SG's 2022 report says most multi-victim 2021 MINUSCA allegations involved one TCC whose troops were repatriated in September 2021, and that 25 allegations in 2021 (all missions) involved 51 children
cases.who: Gabonese military contingent, MINUSCA
cases.d: On 15 September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA (about 450 personnel) would be repatriated after allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse; Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report links most multiple-victim MINUSCA allegations of 2021 to one troop-contributing country repatriated that September.
cases.cite: UN News, 15 Sept 2021; Report of the Secretary-General A/76/702 (2022)

cases.n: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.place: Prijedor, Bijeljina, Tuzla, Arizona Market (Brčko) and other towns
cases.victims_note: HRW cites a programme total of 601 women and girls of whom 498 were repatriated; girls under 18 among them (e.g. a 17-year-old Romanian in Prijedor)
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.cover: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.
cases.d: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cite: Human Rights Watch, 'Hopes Betrayed: Trafficking of Women and Girls to Post-Conflict Bosnia and Herzegovina for Forced Prostitution', Vol. 14 No. 9(D), November 2002; Bolkovac v DynCorp Aerospace Operations (UK) Ltd, Employment Tribunal, 2 Aug 2002

cases.n: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.victims_note: A Kosovo victim-support group reported that of locally trafficked girls a third were under 14 and 80% under 18
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.cover: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.
cases.d: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cite: Amnesty International, 'So does it mean that we have the rights?' (Kosovo), May 2004, as reported by The Guardian, 7 May 2004

cases.n: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
cases.who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
cases.d: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. The 1996 Machel study separately recorded children trafficked from Cambodia to brothels in Thailand. Child-specific findings against UNTAC personnel are not documented in the sources consulted.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'United Nations Transitional Authority in Cambodia' and 'Sexual abuse by UN peacekeepers'; Machel, Impact of Armed Conflict on Children, A/51/306 (1996)

cases.n: ONUMOZ Mozambique — soldiers recruited girls aged 12–18 into prostitution (Machel study)
cases.who: UN Operation in Mozambique (ONUMOZ) soldiers
cases.d: The UN study 'Impact of Armed Conflict on Children' led by Graça Machel (August 1996) found that after the 1992 peace treaty, ONUMOZ soldiers recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. It also found that in 6 of 12 country studies on sexual exploitation of children in armed conflict, the arrival of peacekeeping troops was associated with a rapid rise in child prostitution.
cases.cite: Report of the expert of the Secretary-General, Graça Machel, 'Impact of Armed Conflict on Children', UN doc A/51/306, 26 August 1996

cases.n: Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued
cases.who: Oxfam GB staff in the 2010 earthquake response, including the country director
cases.cover: Staff including the Belgian country director were allowed to resign; Oxfam did not report the allegations of abuse of minors to the Charity Commission or police in 2011.
cases.d: Oxfam GB's 2011 internal investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some of whom were alleged to be 'underage'. The Charity Commission's June 2019 inquiry found that not all lines of enquiry about minors were pursued and that Oxfam did not adequately investigate allegations in an email of 18 July 2011 that minors were being sexually abused by Oxfam employees, nor report them to the Commission or law enforcement. The Commission said it was no longer possible to conclude with certainty whether minors were involved or at risk.
cases.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, Inquiry Report: Oxfam GB — summary findings and conclusions, 11 June 2019

cases.n: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
cases.place: Beni, Butembo, Mangina (North Kivu) and Ituri
cases.victims_note: testimony from 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; nine rape allegations; 29 pregnancies
cases.who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
cases.d: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.
cases.cite: Final Report of the Independent Commission on the review of sexual abuse and exploitation during the response to the 10th Ebola virus disease epidemic in North Kivu and Ituri, DRC, 28 September 2021

cases.n: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
cases.place: AMISOM base camp and Burundian contingent base, Mogadishu
cases.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
cases.d: Human Rights Watch's 71-page report of 8 September 2014 documented AU soldiers on two Mogadishu bases raping women and girls as young as 12 and trading food aid for sex, including women seeking medicine for sick babies. The African Union rejected the findings as isolated cases.
cases.cite: Human Rights Watch, 'The Power These Men Have Over Us', 8 September 2014, as summarised in Wikipedia 'African Union Mission to Somalia'

cases.n: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
cases.victims_note: SIGAR: DoD received 5,753 vetting requests; investigating 75 reports of gross violations, 7 involving child sexual assault
cases.who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
cases.cover: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).
cases.d: In 2011 a Kunduz mother reported that an Afghan Local Police commander had chained her 12-year-old son to a bed and raped him for two weeks; two US Special Forces soldiers who beat the commander were removed, later reinstated. The New York Times reported in September 2015 that US soldiers had been instructed by commanders to ignore child sexual abuse by Afghan allies. The Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction reported in June 2017 that DoD had 75 reports of gross human rights violations under review, 7 involving child sexual assault, and the NYT reported that aid was never cut off to an offending unit.
cases.cite: SIGAR, Child Sexual Assault in Afghanistan: Implementation of the Leahy Laws (SIGAR 17-47-IP), June 2017 (not opened; figures via Wikipedia 'Bacha bazi'); NYT, 20 Sept 2015

cases.n: Myanmar — Tatmadaw sexual violence against Rohingya and ethnic minority women, girls and boys (UN FFM)
cases.place: Northern Rakhine (e.g. Min Gyi/Tula Toli), Kachin and Shan
cases.victims_note: 'Hundreds' of Rohingya women and girls raped; 80% of corroborated rapes were gang rapes
cases.who: Myanmar armed forces (Tatmadaw)
cases.d: The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of corroborated cases being gang rapes, and its August 2019 report found sexual and gender-based violence a 'hallmark' of Tatmadaw operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. It documented Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, detained at Buthidaung prison in 2012 and subjected to sexual violence.
cases.cite: Report of the FFM on Myanmar, A/HRC/39/CRP.2, 17 Sept 2018; 'Sexual and gender-based violence in Myanmar and the gendered impact of its ethnic conflicts', A/HRC/42/CRP.4, 22 Aug 2019

cases.n: Sudan — RSF rape and sexual slavery of women and girls (UN Fact-Finding Mission 2024)
cases.place: Darfur (El Geneina, West Darfur) and Khartoum
cases.victims_note: rape of girls as young as 8 documented; UN verified sexual violence against 114 children in 2023 and 74 in 2024 (most attributed to RSF)
cases.who: Rapid Support Forces and allied militias; also some cases by Sudanese Armed Forces
cases.d: The independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan found that rape and gang rape were widespread, mostly by men in RSF uniform and allied militias, with victims including girls as young as 8. It found the abduction and detention of women and girls for sexual purposes by the RSF amounted to sexual slavery. The UN Secretary-General verified sexual violence against 114 girls in 2023 (RSF 57) and 74 children in 2024 (RSF 54, RSF-affiliated militia 9) and listed the RSF for rape and abduction of children.
cases.cite: Report of the independent international fact-finding mission for the Sudan, A/HRC/57/23, 2024; SG reports on Children and Armed Conflict A/78/842 (2024) and A/79/878 (2025)

cases.n: Ethiopia — Tigray war sexual violence including girls (ICHREE; UN verified)
cases.victims_note: BBC (Feb 2021) reported 200 girls under 18 registered as rape survivors in Mekelle; UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in 2024 (ENDF 38)
cases.who: Ethiopian National Defence Forces, Eritrean Defence Forces, Amhara forces and Tigrayan forces
cases.d: The International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia (October 2022) documented Tigrayan forces' rapes of women and girls as young as 11 in Amhara villages such as Chenna in 2021, alongside widespread sexual violence by Ethiopian and Eritrean forces in Tigray. BBC reported in February 2021 that 200 girls under 18 had registered at Mekelle health facilities as rape survivors. The UN verified sexual violence against 73 children in Ethiopia in 2024, 38 attributed to the ENDF.
cases.cite: Report of the International Commission of Human Rights Experts on Ethiopia, A/HRC/51/46, 5 Oct 2022; Wikipedia 'Sexual violence in the Tigray war'; SG CAAC report A/79/878

cases.n: Ukraine — rape and sexual violence by Russian forces incl. children (UN Commission of Inquiry)
cases.place: Kyiv, Kherson and other formerly occupied areas
cases.victims_note: Ukraine Prosecutor General: 23 children sexually abused (childrenofwar.gov.ua, accessed Oct 2026)
cases.who: Russian armed forces and authorities
cases.d: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed the war crimes of rape and other sexual violence; cases it investigated included a 16-year-old girl, and in September 2022 it said it had documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General.
cases.cite: Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, A/78/540, 19 Oct 2023; A/HRC/52/62; Children of War portal (Govt of Ukraine)

cases.n: Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
cases.place: Occupied Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, Zaporizhzhia and Crimea → Russia
cases.victims_note: Ukraine/Bring Kids Back UA count of deported and/or forcibly displaced children (Oct 2026); 2,752 returned; the UN COI notes Ukraine's figure mixes categories and may include duplicates
cases.who: Russian state: President Vladimir Putin; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.d: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022. The UN Commission of Inquiry found a transfer of 31 children in May 2022 was unlawful deportation and a war crime; Lvova-Belova's own bulletin said 380 orphans had been placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children from institutions transferred in February 2022. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for 're-education'.
cases.cite: ICC press release, 17 March 2023; COI Ukraine A/78/540 (2023); Children of War portal; Yale HRL / Conflict Observatory report, 14 Feb 2023 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: China — Uyghur children separated from detained parents and placed in state boarding schools
cases.victims_note: NYT (Dec 2019) reported about 497,000 elementary and junior high pupils enrolled in such boarding schools
cases.who: Chinese state authorities in Xinjiang
cases.d: Detention of Uyghur and other minority adults in Xinjiang left many children without parents; AP reported in September 2018 that thousands of boarding schools were being built, and the BBC and researcher Adrian Zenz reported in 2019 that children in them were penalised for not speaking Mandarin. Human Rights Watch said children were held at welfare facilities and boarding schools without parental consent. The New York Times reported about 497,000 pupils enrolled in December 2019. China denies the allegations. No sexual-abuse finding is recorded here; this is a child-removal record.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Xinjiang internment camps' (citing AP Sept 2018, BBC 2019, HRW, NYT Dec 2019)

cases.n: Okinawa — rape of a 12-year-old girl by three US servicemen (1995)
cases.who: US Navy and Marine Corps personnel from Camp Hansen
cases.d: On 4 September 1995 three US servicemen based at Camp Hansen abducted and raped a 12-year-old Okinawan girl. They were tried in a Japanese court under the US–Japan Status of Forces Agreement; in 1996 two were sentenced to seven years and one to six and a half years. The case triggered mass protests against the US bases.
cases.cite: Wikipedia '1995 Okinawa rape incident'

cases.n: Bosnia — Foča rape camps; ICTY Kunarac judgment (girls as young as 12 enslaved)
cases.who: Bosnian Serb army (VRS) and paramilitaries; local police chief named in testimony
cases.d: In Serb-held Foča, Bosniak women and girls, including minors as young as 12, were held in detention sites such as 'Karaman's house' and repeatedly raped. The ICTY convicted Dragoljub Kunarac (28 years' imprisonment for rape, torture and enslavement) and Radomir Kovač (20 years), who had raped a 12-year-old girl and then sold her into slavery; the Kunarac trial was the first conviction anywhere for using rape as a weapon of war. Witnesses identified the Foča police chief as visiting the camps to select women.
cases.cite: ICTY, Prosecutor v. Kunarac, Kovač and Vuković (via Wikipedia 'Rape during the Bosnian War')

cases.n: Israel/Gaza — UN COI findings on sexual violence incl. against Palestinian boys and on 7 October
cases.place: Gaza Strip, West Bank and southern Israel
cases.victims_note: 7 Oct 2023: 36 children among 252 hostages (COI)
cases.who: Israeli security forces (detention and arrest); Hamas and other armed groups (7 October)
cases.d: The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that 'men and boys were targeted in particular ways'; it found gender persecution of Palestinian men and boys as a crime against humanity. It also found sexual violence was committed on 7 October 2023 at the Nova festival, Nahal Oz and several kibbutzim, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage. Recorded only to the extent of these UN findings.
cases.cite: Report of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the OPT and Israel, A/HRC/56/26, 14 June 2024

cases.n: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls
cases.place: Sinjar, Ninewa → Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush, Galaxy hall), Raqqa
cases.victims_note: COI 2016: over 3,200 Yazidi women and children still held; UN estimate cited of about 7,000 women and girls kidnapped; PLOS Medicine 2017 survey estimated 4,200–10,800 abducted
cases.who: Islamic State (ISIS/Da'esh)
cases.d: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 ('They came to destroy') that ISIS committed genocide; women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date over 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria; thousands remain missing.
cases.cite: Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Syrian Arab Republic, 'They came to destroy': ISIS Crimes Against the Yazidis, A/HRC/32/CRP.2, 15 June 2016

cases.n: Chibok schoolgirls abduction — Boko Haram
cases.place: Government Girls Secondary School, Chibok, Borno
cases.victims_note: 276 abducted (police figure); 57 escaped immediately; 82 still captive as of April 2024 (Amnesty)
cases.who: Boko Haram (JAS)
cases.d: On 14–15 April 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok, according to the local police; 57 escaped by jumping from the trucks, and the rest were believed taken to camps including the Sambisa Forest. Most later releases came via negotiated deals. Amnesty International said that on the tenth anniversary in April 2024, 82 girls remained in captivity, and estimated in 2015 that at least 2,000 women and girls had been abducted by the group since 2014, many forced into sexual slavery.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Chibok schoolgirls kidnapping' (citing Amnesty International, 14 April 2024)

cases.n: Dapchi schoolgirls abduction — ISWAP/Boko Haram
cases.place: Government Girls Science and Technical College, Dapchi, Yobe
cases.victims_note: 110 girls unaccounted for (Nigerian minister); 5 died on the day; 104 schoolgirls returned 21 March 2018; one (Christian) girl still held
cases.who: Boko Haram faction (ISWAP)
cases.d: On 19 February 2018 militants abducted about 110 girls from a school in Dapchi. On 21 March 2018 the Nigerian government said 106 children, including 104 schoolgirls, had been returned; five girls died on the day of the abduction. One Christian girl, aged 14 at capture, who refused to convert, remained in captivity. An army intelligence document of 6 February 2018 had warned of a possible attack nearby.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Dapchi schoolgirls kidnapping'

cases.n: Kankara schoolboys abduction (Katsina, 2020)
cases.place: Government Science Secondary School, Kankara, Katsina
cases.victims_note: 344 freed on 17 Dec 2020 per state governor
cases.who: Armed bandits; Boko Haram's Shekau claimed responsibility
cases.d: On 11 December 2020 over 300 pupils were kidnapped from a boys' boarding school in Kankara. Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau claimed the abduction in an audio message; on 17 December the Katsina governor said 344 boys had been freed from a forest in Zamfara State.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Kankara kidnapping'

cases.n: Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024)
cases.victims_note: 991 children abducted (637 girls); sexual violence (all forced marriage) against 419 children (412 girls) verified in 2024
cases.who: Jama'atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'Awati Wal-Jihad (JAS/Boko Haram), ISWAP, Bakura
cases.d: The UN verified the abduction of 991 children (354 boys, 637 girls) in Nigeria in 2024 by JAS (690), ISWAP (294) and Bakura (7), most for recruitment and use. It also verified sexual violence, all involving forced marriage, against 419 children (7 boys, 412 girls) by JAS (304), ISWAP (114) and Bakura (1). In 2023 the UN had verified sexual violence against 366 children following abduction.
cases.cite: Report of the Secretary-General, Children and armed conflict, A/79/878-S/2025/247, 17 June 2025, paras 310–312

cases.n: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.place: Northern Uganda (Acholiland: Gulu, Lukodi, Pajule, Odek, Abok)
cases.victims_note: UNICEF estimated (2006) at least 25,000 children abducted; other estimates over 50,000 children captured in 20 years
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.d: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.
cases.cite: ICC, The Prosecutor v. Dominic Ongwen, ICC-02/04-01/15 (case information page); Wikipedia 'Lord's Resistance Army'

cases.n: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
cases.victims_note: 250 abducted (adults and children), at least 321 killed
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army forces under Dominic Ongwen
cases.d: In December 2009 LRA forces under Dominic Ongwen killed at least 321 civilians and abducted 250 people during a four-day attack in the Makombo area of north-eastern DR Congo. Between September 2008 and July 2011 the LRA abducted more than 3,000 people across DR Congo, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Lord's Resistance Army' (citing HRW reporting)

cases.n: Colombia — FARC-EP recruitment and use of children (JEP Macro-case 07)
cases.place: Colombia (Bloque Oriental and Bloque Sur areas)
cases.victims_note: provisional universe of 18,677 unique victims (JEP, Aug 2021); 9,854 accredited
cases.who: Former FARC-EP secretariat and commanders
cases.d: The Special Jurisdiction for Peace's Case 07 investigates the recruitment and use of children by the former FARC-EP; in August 2021 it identified a provisional universe of 18,677 unique victims and has accredited 9,854. The JEP indicted former FARC-EP commanders for war crimes including the recruitment and use of children and sexual violence against children, and has referred a former FARC member accused of reproductive violence against recruited girls to its investigation unit. Former secretariat members have publicly acknowledged responsibility.

cases.n: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
cases.place: Colonia Dignidad (now Villa Baviera), Parral, Maule region
cases.kind: sexual abuse + forced labour + child removal
cases.victims_note: 2006 conviction covered 25 minors abused 1993–1997; about 100 children lived in the colony; children were brought from Germany
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cases.cover: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.
cases.d: German preacher Paul Schäfer, who left Germany in 1961 after accusations of molesting children, ran the colony, separating children from parents. Chile's National Commission for Truth and Reconciliation (Rettig, 1991) found evidence that the colony's land was used by DINA, Pinochet's secret police, for the detention and torture of political prisoners; former DINA agent Michael Townley confirmed the DINA link in 2005. A warrant was issued in 1996 after 26 children who attended the colony's school and clinic reported abuse; on 24 May 2006 Schäfer was sentenced to 20 years for 20 counts of indecent assault and 5 of forced sodomy against 25 minors between 1993 and 1997. He died in prison in 2010.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Colonia Dignidad' and 'Paul Schäfer' (citing Rettig Commission 1991, Chilean court 2006); German Wikipedia 'Colonia Dignidad' (Steinmeier file release April 2016; Gauck July 2016; Bundestag resolution 29 June 2017)

cases.n: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity
cases.place: Kincora Boys' Home, Upper Newtownards Road, east Belfast
cases.who: Kincora staff (William McGrath, Raymond Semple, Joseph Mains — convicted 1981); alleged: MI5, army intelligence, RUC Special Branch
cases.cover: Abuse allegations reached the RUC by 1977 without prosecution until 1980; the Hart inquiry found a 'catalogue of failures' by police and authorities. Former army officers Colin Wallace and Brian Gemmell said in 2014 that superiors stopped them passing on or pursuing information.
cases.d: Three Kincora staff were convicted in 1981 of systematic sexual abuse of boys in their care. For decades it was alleged that McGrath, leader of the loyalist group Tara, was an MI5 agent and that intelligence services protected a ring of prominent abusers to blackmail them. On 20 January 2017 the Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hart found 'no credible evidence' that others were involved or that 'the security agencies were complicit in any form of sexual abuse in Kincora for any purpose', and said the 'honey pot' blackmail claim was without foundation; it said the government's promise to hand over all files had been honoured. In June 2025 former resident Gary Hoy settled his civil claim against the PSNI and Home Secretary, which alleged McGrath was protected as an MI5 agent, on confidential terms with no admission of liability.
cases.cite: Northern Ireland Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry report (Hart), 20 Jan 2017, as reported by RTÉ News, 20 Jan 2017; RTÉ News, 16 June 2025

cases.n: Duplessis Orphans (Quebec) — healthy orphans falsely certified mentally ill and confined
cases.place: Quebec psychiatric hospitals and orphanages (e.g. Mont-Providence, Montreal)
cases.victims_note: about 3,000 survivors in the Duplessis Orphans Committee in the 1990s; 240 orphans made 321 criminal complaints
cases.who: Government of Quebec under Maurice Duplessis; Catholic religious orders running orphanages and hospitals
cases.cover: No criminal charges resulted from the 1990s complaints; the 2001 compensation excluded victims of sexual or other abuse.
cases.d: Under Premier Maurice Duplessis, many healthy children in Quebec orphanages were classified as mentally ill and sent to psychiatric hospitals because federal subsidies paid more for psychiatric patients ($2.75 a day) than orphans ($1.25); an early-1960s commission found one third of 22,000 patients were classified for financial reasons. Many survivors say they were physically and sexually abused and subjected to lobotomies, electroshock and straitjackets. Premier Lucien Bouchard apologised on 4 March 1999, and in 2001 Quebec offered about $25,000 per orphan, not covering sexual or other abuse. Claims linking the orphans to CIA MKUltra experiments are not established by the sources consulted.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Duplessis Orphans' (citing CBC, 8 March 1999 and 1 July 2001)

cases.n: Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) / Patriotic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (FPLC)
cases.d: On 8 July 2019 ICC Trial Chamber VI found Bosco Ntaganda guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Ituri in 2002–2003, including rape, sexual slavery and the conscription and use of children under 15; he was the first person convicted of sexual slavery by the ICC. He was sentenced to 30 years on 7 November 2019, confirmed on appeal on 30 March 2021. He had told child soldiers, 'When you're a soldier, you get a woman for free'.
cases.cite: ICC case page, The Prosecutor v. Bosco Ntaganda; Wikipedia 'Bosco Ntaganda'

cases.n: Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children

Global 2024 total: 4,573 abductions; 2022: 1,165 children subjected to sexual violence.

notes:
SCOPE AND METHOD. All cases are drawn from documents opened in this session: UN Secretary-General reports (documents.un.org PDFs), UN Commissions of Inquiry / fact-finding missions, ICC case pages, the WHO Independent Commission report, the UK Charity Commission Oxfam report, HRW reports, RTÉ, UN News, the Ukrainian government Children of War portal, and Wikipedia (English, French, German) where primary pages were blocked. The web-search budget for the session ran out early, so later material came from direct fetches of known URLs.

BLOCKED / NOT OPENED (verify before publishing): conduct.unmissions.org (403/permission timeout) — so 2017+ per-nationality SEA data and the official SEA dashboard were not used; SIGAR 17-47-IP (sigar.mil refused by proxy; SIGAR figures 5,753 vetting requests / 75 gross-violation reports / 7 child sexual assault are taken from Wikipedia 'Bacha bazi'); AP 2017 Haiti investigation (apnews.com blocked; figures via Wikipedia); Reuters (blocked) — the Reuters 2022 investigation into the Nigerian military's secret abortion programme and Amnesty's 2018 Bama/Banki report were NOT verified and are NOT recorded; the Deschamps independent panel report on CAR (2015) — UN URL returned 404, not recorded as its own case; HIA Inquiry Kincora chapter PDF (server reset) — Hart findings taken from RTÉ News 20 Jan 2017; Yale HRL report (conflictobservatory reset) — 43 camps/6,000 children figure via Wikipedia; HRW AMISOM report page 404 — via Wikipedia summary.

INTELLIGENCE / SECURITY-SERVICE CLAIMS — STATUS:
- PROVEN (official finding): Colonia Dignidad was used by DINA (Chile's secret police) as a detention and torture site (Rettig Commission 1991; Townley 2005). Schäfer was convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 minors; the abuse of children is proven, and the state/intelligence link is proven as to political prisoners. No source found that DINA itself took part in the child abuse. German state failures were acknowledged (President Gauck, July 2016; Bundestag resolution 29 June 2017).
- PROVEN (policy-level): US forces in Afghanistan were told not to intervene in child sexual abuse by Afghan allies (NYT 2015, court records); SIGAR 2017 confirmed child sexual assault cases among gross violations under Leahy review. This is a finding of tolerance and inaction, not of US personnel committing abuse.
- PROVEN: Bosnia — local police were directly involved in trafficking, and IPTF monitors and DynCorp contractors bought trafficked women and girls (HRW 2002, US Army CID); UN immunity and repatriation prevented prosecution. The employment tribunal found DynCorp unfairly dismissed whistleblower Bolkovac (2002).
- DISPROVED (by official inquiry): Kincora — the HIA Inquiry (Hart, 20 Jan 2017) found no credible evidence that MI5, army intelligence or RUC Special Branch were complicit in, knew of, or used the abuse for blackmail. Still disputed: Colin Wallace's and Brian Gemmell's accounts (2014); Gary Hoy's civil claim settled in June 2025 with no admission of liability; Chris Moore's 2025 book allegations about Mountbatten. These are unresolved allegations, not findings. A UK Supreme Court challenge by Hoy over the inquiry's powers failed (2016). The brief mentioned a possible 2022 Court of Appeal ruling; none was found — only a 2022 writ by Arthur Smyth.
- NOT ESTABLISHED: Duplessis Orphans — state-run wrongful psychiatric confinement is acknowledged (Bouchard apology 1999; 2001 compensation). Survivors allege sexual abuse; no sexual-abuse finding was made and compensation excluded it. No source links the orphans to CIA MKUltra (the Allan Memorial/Cameron experiments were mostly on adults; a 2025 Quebec class action includes a survivor admitted at 15).
- Skipped per brief: Dutroux, Epstein, Franklin (elite agent), Gladio, JITEM, the apartheid 'Aversion Project'.

FRENCH SANGARIS: recorded as 'alleged'. Paris judges dismissed the case on 11 Jan 2018 (non-lieu) for insufficient charges; the prosecutor said it could not be affirmed that no abuse occurred. An October 2016 UN conduct report and OIOS interim findings questioned some testimony (possible false statements for compensation) in the Dékoa allegations against Burundian and Gabonese peacekeepers and French soldiers. The map should show both.

SERIES CAVEATS: un_sea 2004–2009 counts DPKO/DFS personnel as reported to OIOS; 2010+ counts peacekeeping plus special political missions. The 2005 figure (340) comes from A/67/766's retrospective; A/60/861 gives 373 for all entities. Child-victim figures appear in the reports only from 2015. The 2022 child-victim number was revised from 26 (A/77/748) to 35 (A/78/774). The un_sea_by_tcc 2016 rows were parsed automatically from the annex table; spot-check them against the PDF (DRC 17/15; Burundi 4/46; Gabon 4/43; Congo 9/7; Morocco 7/6; South Africa 7/1). caac_verified rows were parsed by regex from the CAAC reports; nulls mean 'not extracted', not zero.

GAPS / LEADS: Liberia UNMIL and Sierra Leone UNAMSIL child cases (beyond the 2002 report); MINUSTAH Uruguayan contingent (Port-Salut, 2011) — no source opened; Nigerian military IDP-camp sexual exploitation (Amnesty 2018) and the abortion programme (Reuters 2022) — need sources; Colombia: the 2015 Historical Memory Commission (Melgar/Girardot) report on US military contractors' abuse of girls was not found in any source opened (the es-wiki pages do not exist), so it is not recorded; North Korea: no child sexual-abuse finding located (the UN COI 2014 covers trafficking of women to China — lead); El Fasher (Oct 2025) child sexual-violence figures not yet in the reports opened; Gaza 2025 'sex for aid' (AP) concerns women — not recorded. Global facts usable as context: 527 children reported born of SEA in UN missions since 2010 (A/78/774); 750 paternity claims 2006–Jan 2025, 517 pending (A/79/789); UN verified 4,573 child abductions worldwide in 2024 (A/79/878).
